lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: When you sell gold, the buyer will test it. If you don't know the purity, you will be cheated. In Africa, many small-scale miners sell raw gold at 50-70% of its true value because they cannot prove its fineness. Assaying is the process of determining how much pure gold is in your sample. It matters because a 1-gram difference in purity on a 100-gram sale can mean hundreds of dollars lost. For example, if gold is 18 karat (75% pure) and you sell it as 22 karat (91.6% pure), you lose about $300 on a 100-gram sale at $60 per gram. Assaying also helps you control your smelting process. If you smelt and the assay shows 85% purity, you know you need to improve your flux or remove more base metals. In Africa, common impurities are silver, copper, and iron. These affect color, hardness, and value. A simple assay can be done with a touchstone and acids, or more accurately with a fire assay or electronic tester. This module will teach you practical methods that work in a small workshop, using locally available materials. You will learn to take a proper sample, test it, and calculate purity. You will also learn to avoid common mistakes like testing dirty metal or using wrong acids. By the end, you will be able to determine the purity of your gold within 1-2% accuracy using basic tools. That knowledge protects your income and helps you negotiate better prices. Remember: never sell gold without knowing its purity. Always assay before you sell or smelt.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To assay gold, you need a few basic tools. For the touchstone method, you need a black touchstone (basalt or slate), a set of test acids (nitric acid, hydrochloric acid, and aqua regia), and gold test needles of known purity (e.g., 8K, 14K, 18K, 22K, 24K). In Africa, you can buy these from jewelry supply shops in cities like Nairobi, Accra, or Johannesburg. A small acid test kit costs about $50-$100. For fire assay, you need a crucible, furnace (or charcoal forge), lead foil, cupel (bone ash cup), and a balance accurate to 0.01 grams. A digital pocket scale costs $20-$40. You also need safety gear: goggles, gloves, and a respirator. For electronic testing, a gold tester (e.g., Kee Gold Tester) costs $200-$500 and uses a probe and gel. It gives a digital reading. For sampling, you need a small hammer, chisel, and file. Always use a clean file to avoid contamination. For weighing, a 0.01g scale is enough for small lots. For larger lots, use a 0.1g scale. You also need a notebook to record results. In rural areas, you can improvise: use a dark ceramic tile as a touchstone, and buy acids from chemical suppliers. But be careful: acids are dangerous. Store them in glass bottles with tight caps, away from children. For fire assay, you can build a small furnace from a metal bucket and charcoal, but you need a crucible that withstands 1200Â°C. Clay crucibles work. Cupels can be made from bone ash or bought. A balance can be a simple beam scale, but digital is better. Always calibrate your scale with a known weight. These tools will let you assay gold accurately without a lab.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Here is a practical step-by-step method for assaying gold using the touchstone method, which is cheap and works in the field. First, clean your gold sample by rubbing it with a file or sandpaper to remove dirt and oxide. Then, rub the gold firmly on the touchstone to leave a clear streak. Do this for your sample and for each test needle. Now, apply a drop of nitric acid to the streaks. Nitric acid dissolves silver and base metals but not gold. If the streak disappears, it is not gold. If it remains, gold is present. Next, apply aqua regia (3 parts hydrochloric acid to 1 part nitric acid) to the streaks. Aqua regia dissolves gold. Compare how fast the streak dissolves with the test needles. The needle that dissolves at the same rate as your sample indicates the purity. For example, if your sample dissolves like the 18K needle, it is about 18K (75% pure). For more accuracy, use the fire assay method. Weigh 0.5g of your sample and 2g of lead foil. Wrap the sample in lead and place in a cupel. Heat in a furnace at 1000Â°C for 1 hour. Lead oxidizes and absorbs into the cupel, leaving a gold-silver bead. Weigh the bead. Then, separate silver by boiling in nitric acid. The remaining gold is pure. Calculate purity: (weight of pure gold / original sample weight) x 100. For example, if 0.5g sample yields 0.45g pure gold, purity is 90%. For electronic testing, clean the sample, apply a drop of gel, and touch the probe. The reading shows karat or percentage. Always test three spots on the sample and average. Record all results. This method gives you reliable purity data.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many learners make mistakes that lead to wrong assay results. Here are the most common and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Testing dirty gold. Dirt, oil, or oxide gives false readings. Fix: Always clean the sample with a file or sandpaper until it shines. Mistake 2: Using old or contaminated acids. Acids absorb moisture and lose strength. Fix: Store acids in tight glass bottles and replace every 6 months. Mistake 3: Not using a control. Without a known purity needle, you cannot compare. Fix: Always use at least three test needles (e.g., 14K, 18K, 22K) and include a known sample. Mistake 4: Rubbing too hard on touchstone. This creates a thick streak that dissolves slowly. Fix: Use light, even pressure to make a thin, uniform streak. Mistake 5: Ignoring temperature in fire assay. Too hot or too cold gives incomplete separation. Fix: Use a furnace with a thermostat set to 1000Â°C. If using charcoal, use a pyrometer or watch for cherry-red heat. Mistake 6: Not weighing accurately. A 0.01g error on a 0.5g sample is 2% error. Fix: Use a calibrated digital scale and weigh three times. Mistake 7: Testing only one spot. Gold can be uneven. Fix: Test three spots and average. Mistake 8: Using wrong acid ratio for aqua regia. Too much nitric acid dissolves gold too fast. Fix: Mix 3 parts HCl to 1 part HNO3 by volume. Mistake 9: Not recording results. You forget and repeat mistakes. Fix: Keep a logbook with date, sample ID, method, and result. Mistake 10: Skipping safety gear. Acids burn skin and eyes. Fix: Always wear goggles, gloves, and apron. By avoiding these mistakes, your assay will be accurate and safe.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Assaying gold involves dangerous chemicals and high heat. Safety is not optional. Always wear personal protective equipment (PPE): safety goggles, nitrile gloves, and a rubber apron. Work in a well-ventilated area, preferably outdoors or with a fume hood. Nitric acid and aqua regia produce toxic fumes. Never breathe them. If you smell fumes, step away and improve ventilation. Store acids in glass bottles with tight caps, in a locked cabinet away from metals and organic matter. Never store acids in metal containers. When mixing aqua regia, always add acid to water, never water to acid. Mix slowly in a glass beaker. Have a bucket of clean water and baking soda nearby to neutralize spills. If acid touches skin, rinse with plenty of water for 15 minutes. If it gets in eyes, rinse and seek medical help. For fire assay, use tongs and heat-resistant gloves. The furnace is 1000Â°C. Keep flammable materials away. Never leave a hot furnace unattended. Use a proper crucible and cupel; cracked ones can explode. After use, let everything cool before handling. Best practice: work in pairs, never alone. Keep a first aid kit with burn cream and eye wash. Label all chemicals clearly. Do not eat, drink, or smoke in the assay area. Wash hands after work. Dispose of waste properly: neutralize acids with baking soda before disposal. Never pour acids down the drain. For electronic testers, follow the manufacturer's instructions and replace gel regularly. Finally, keep good records: date, sample, method, result, and any issues. This helps you improve and stay safe. Remember, a safe assay is a good assay.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to practice. This exercise will guide you through assaying a gold sample using the touchstone method. You will need: a gold sample (at least 0.5g), a touchstone, test acids (nitric and aqua regia), test needles (14K, 18K, 22K), a file, a digital scale (0.01g), and safety gear. Step 1: Clean your gold sample with a file until it is shiny. Weigh it and record the weight. Step 2: Rub the sample on the touchstone to make a streak about 2cm long. Do the same with each test needle. Step 3: Apply one drop of nitric acid to each streak. Wait 30 seconds. The streaks that remain are gold. The ones that disappear are not. Step 4: Apply one drop of aqua regia to each remaining streak. Watch how fast they dissolve. The streak that dissolves at the same rate as the 18K needle indicates your sample is about 18K. Step 5: Repeat the test three times on different spots of your sample. Average your observations. Step 6: Calculate purity. If your sample matches 18K, purity is 75%. If it matches 22K, purity is 91.6%. Record your result. For a more accurate result, use the fire assay method: weigh 0.5g sample, wrap in 2g lead foil, cupel at 1000Â°C for 1 hour, weigh the bead, then boil in nitric acid to remove silver, weigh pure gold, and calculate percentage. Do this exercise with three different gold samples (e.g., from different mines or batches). Compare results. Write a short report: sample ID, weight, method, purity, and any observations. This exercise will build your confidence. Remember, practice makes perfect. The more you assay, the better you get. Share your results with your mentor or classmates for feedback.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to assay gold before selling?
options: B) To know its purity and avoid being cheated
quiz.explanation: Assaying determines purity, which directly affects the price you get.

quiz.q: Which acid dissolves gold?
quiz.explanation: Aqua regia, a mix of nitric and hydrochloric acid, dissolves gold.

quiz.q: What is a touchstone used for?
options: B) Testing gold purity by streak
quiz.explanation: A touchstone is a black stone on which gold leaves a streak for acid testing.

quiz.q: What does 18 karat gold mean?
quiz.explanation: 18K is 18/24 = 75% pure gold.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for accurate weighing in assay?
quiz.explanation: A digital scale accurate to 0.01g is needed for precise purity calculations.

quiz.q: In fire assay, what is the purpose of lead foil?
options: C) To make the sample heavier
quiz.explanation: Lead oxidizes and absorbs base metals, leaving a gold-silver bead.

quiz.q: What should you do before testing a gold sample?
options: B) Clean it with a file
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes dirt and oxide that can give false readings.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common mistake in assaying?
quiz.explanation: Gold can be uneven, so testing multiple spots gives a more accurate average.

quiz.q: What is the correct ratio for aqua regia?
options: A) 1 part HCl to 3 parts HNO3
B) 3 parts HCl to 1 part HNO3
C) 1 part HCl to 1 part HNO3
D) 2 parts HCl to 1 part HNO3
quiz.explanation: Aqua regia is typically 3 parts hydrochloric acid to 1 part nitric acid.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important during assay?
quiz.explanation: Acids produce toxic fumes that can harm your lungs.

quiz.q: What should you do if acid touches your skin?
options: B) Rinse with water for 15 minutes
quiz.explanation: Immediate and thorough rinsing with water minimizes acid burns.

quiz.q: What is a cupel made of?
quiz.explanation: Cupels are made of bone ash, which absorbs lead oxide during fire assay.

quiz.q: In fire assay, at what temperature is the cupel heated?
quiz.explanation: Around 1000Â°C is needed for proper oxidation and absorption.

quiz.q: What does a gold tester use to measure purity?
quiz.explanation: Electronic gold testers use a probe and conductive gel to measure purity.

quiz.q: Why should you calibrate your scale?
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures the scale gives correct weights, which is critical for purity calculations.

quiz.q: Which of these is a best practice for storing acids?
options: B) In glass bottles with tight caps
quiz.explanation: Glass bottles with tight caps prevent leaks and contamination.

quiz.q: What should you do with acid waste?
quiz.explanation: Neutralizing with baking soda makes the waste safe for disposal.

quiz.q: How many test needles should you use for comparison?
quiz.explanation: Using at least three needles helps bracket the purity accurately.

quiz.q: What is the purity of 22 karat gold?
quiz.explanation: 22K is 22/24 = 91.6% pure gold.

quiz.q: In the practical exercise, how many times should you repeat the touchstone test?
quiz.explanation: Testing three times on different spots gives a more reliable average.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the touchstone method?
quiz.explanation: You must first rub the gold on the touchstone to create a streak.

quiz.q: Which acid is used to dissolve silver in fire assay?
quiz.explanation: Nitric acid dissolves silver but not gold, allowing separation.

quiz.q: What does a streak that disappears in nitric acid indicate?
quiz.explanation: Nitric acid dissolves base metals and silver, so if the streak disappears, it is not gold.

quiz.q: Why is it important to work in pairs during assay?
options: B) For safety in case of accidents
quiz.explanation: Having a partner ensures someone can help in case of chemical spills or burns.

quiz.q: What should you do before using a digital scale?
quiz.explanation: Calibration ensures accurate measurements.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common impurity in African gold?
quiz.explanation: Platinum is rare in most African gold; silver, copper, and iron are common.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fume hood?
quiz.explanation: A fume hood ventilates dangerous fumes away from the user.

quiz.q: How can you improvise a touchstone in rural areas?
options: B) Use a dark ceramic tile
quiz.explanation: A dark ceramic tile can serve as a touchstone for streak testing.

quiz.q: What is the formula to calculate purity percentage?
options: A) (weight of pure gold / original sample weight) x 100
B) (original weight / pure gold weight) x 100
C) (pure gold weight x original weight) / 100
D) (pure gold weight + original weight) x 100
quiz.explanation: Purity percentage is the ratio of pure gold to original sample weight, times 100.

quiz.q: Why should you record assay results?
options: B) To track and improve your process
quiz.explanation: Records help you identify trends, avoid mistakes, and improve smelting.
